title: Training and office hours
bridge: The trainings are like pairing on a team's code review habits, run once for everyone and recorded. Except: every question people ask goes back into the tools. A weak plan becomes an eval case, and a confusing answer becomes a skill line or a brain page.
intro: Skills help only if people use the habits behind them. G8 ends with four hands-on trainings and a weekly drop-in from W6 to W12. This lesson walks through what each session teaches, how to run it on seed data, and how its questions feed the evals.

picture.caption: Sessions teach the habits; their questions come back as eval cases, skill lines and brain pages.

nodes.label: Eval cases for verify and plan-and-grill

steps.text: run a hands-on session on one habit
practise on seed data: plant a bug, write a plan, hand a ticket to Nova
record it; put slides and recording in Drive Rhino Team/Engineering
a brain page links the recording
the questions people struggled with become eval cases
office hours collect what is still confusing, every week

p: Four trainings and one recurring slot.

Training 1 (G8-14) is the verify habit. Training 2 (G8-17) is plan mode and the grill. Training 3 (G8-20) is running many agents at once. Training 4 (G8-21) is working with Nova. Office hours (G8-15) run weekly from W6 to W12.

Each session is hands-on, uses seed data, is recorded, and is linked from a brain page. And each one feeds the tools: the questions people struggled with become eval cases or brain pages. That loop is why the trainings sit in G8 with the skills, not in a separate HR plan.

callout.text: Seed data only, in every exercise. PHI never enters a prompt, so no session uses production data or real customer rows.

sections.h: Training 1: checks before code, proof not claims (G8-14)
p: A 45-minute session for all engineers on the verify habit (lesson g8-2). Choose the checks before coding, plant a bug to prove a check can fail, and record proof. Prepare one FE and one BE exercise in FCP Lab: a small real bug from Jira, already fixed on a branch.

Show a PR written with proof next to one written with claims. Then let people plant a bug and watch a weak test still pass. That moment teaches more than any slide. The lab below is that exercise on a laptop.
sections.because: We keep the session plan as a short file next to the recording, so the next trainer can run it again.

code.file: Drive: Rhino Team/Engineering/training-1/plan.md (a sketch from the ticket's steps)
code.text:
# Training 1: checks before code, proof not claims (45 min)

1. Two PRs side by side: one with proof, one with claims (5 min)
2. Pick the checks before coding, with the verify skill (10 min)
3. Plant a bug; watch a weak test still pass, then a good one fail (15 min)
4. Record proof: video, screenshots at 760 and 1440, or text (10 min)
5. Questions; note the 3 hardest ones for verify's eval cases (5 min)

notes.text: The title and the length the ticket gives.
Start with the contrast; people see why before how.
The plan-first habit, using the verify skill.
The core exercise: a weak test passes on broken code.
The proof formats the verify skill names.
The 3 questions people struggled with become eval cases for verify.

sections.h: Training 2: plan mode and the grill (G8-17)
p: Plan mode is a Claude Code mode where the agent reads and plans but does not edit until you approve. This session teaches planning before code with plan mode and the plan-and-grill skill. It covers when to ask the requester first, and how to write checks a reviewer trusts.

Use two real tickets. A vague one, where the grill asks questions first, and a small clear one that goes straight to a plan. People work in pairs. Each pair writes a plan with plan mode and the skill, then swaps and reviews the other pair's checks and edge cases.

Show the same plan format Nova posts in Jira and Slack, so people know what they will approve later. Record it, link it from the brain, and add the weak plans people wrote as eval cases for plan-and-grill.

sections.h: Training 3: many agents, sized on purpose (G8-20)
p: Many agents help when the work splits into independent, checkable pieces, and hurt on step-by-step work. One review once started 221 agents and burned about 47M tokens. The session teaches when to fan out and how to keep it sane. A git worktree gives each agent its own checkout, so two tickets do not collide.

Exercises in fcp: two tickets in two worktrees, and a background agent running tests. Then a read-only review workflow with lenses and a skeptic per finding, and a sized prompt. Show /usage and the status line, so each person sees their own spend. No new per-person caps; Anthropic's defaults stay.
sections.because: We put the size in the prompt as guidance, because it steers the fan-out without cutting any run short.

code.file: Training 3 cheat sheet (from the ticket's steps)
code.text:
Sized prompt: audit unused exports in frontend/src, about 10 agents, +300k
One writer per change.
Fan out for research, review and tests.
Stay with one agent for a chain of dependent steps.

notes.text: A size and a token budget in the prompt: about 10 agents and about 300k tokens. This is a person's own session in the training, not an agent run. It guides; nothing stops the run at that number.
Two agents never edit the same change.
Independent, checkable work is where many agents pay off.
Step-by-step work, where each step needs the last, stays with one agent.

callout.text: Guide, don't cage: the platform never cuts a run with a turn, time or budget limit. Training people to size work on purpose is the human side of the same rule.

p: Nova helps only if people give it good tickets and review its PRs well. Walk one pilot ticket end to end on seed data. Assign it to Nova, read the plan in Slack, and press Approve, Change or Stop. Then read the draft PR with proof, Byte's review, and the approval by someone other than the requester.

Show how to read the PR story, the checks table and the receipt, and what a scope-judge veto looks like. Say when not to use Nova: vague work with no owner, or anything that needs production data. Record it and add an FAQ page to the brain. This session needs the G4 pilot to be live.

callout.text: The requester never approves their own agent's PR; exactly one approval from someone else. Every reviewer needs to know what to look for, which is why this training is for everyone.

p: People get stuck on small things, like a skill that does not fire or a plugin that will not install. A fixed 30-minute slot from W6 to W12 unblocks them fast and shows Platform what to fix in the tools. Shai and Platform alternate; post a reminder in a public engineering channel.
Share Harness Lab, the 20-chapter course, as self-study with a suggested order, linked from the brain. Report the top 3 themes in the weekly run review.
sections.because: We log what each question should become, because most point at a missing skill line, eval case or brain page.

| Date | Question | Answer | Becomes |
|------|----------|--------|---------|
| W6 | verify does not fire after an edit | description lacked "after editing code" | skill line + eval case |

notes.text: Four columns: when, what was asked, what we answered, and what it becomes.
A made-up example: a skill that did not fire becomes a description fix and an eval case.
Another made-up example: an install problem becomes a brain page.

p: Every session ends the same way. Record it, put the slides and recording in Drive under Rhino Team/Engineering, and link them from a brain page. Then turn the questions into tools.

Training 1's hardest questions become eval cases for verify. Training 2's weak plans become eval cases for plan-and-grill. Training 3's and 4's questions become eval cases or brain pages. Office hours feed all three kinds of fix. The monthly rule diet (lesson g8-1) then checks that the added lines still earn their place.

lab.title: Run Training 1's exercise and Training 3's worktrees on a scratch repo

worked.do: mkdir lab85 && cd lab85 && git init -q -b main . && uv init --python 3.13 --bare . && uv add --dev pytest

Create test_weak.py:

from discount import price_after_discount


def test_returns_a_number():
    assert isinstance(price_after_discount(100, 20), float)

and test_strong.py:

import pytest

from discount import price_after_discount


def test_twenty_percent_off():
    assert price_after_discount(100, 20) == 80.0


def test_over_100_percent_is_refused():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        price_after_discount(100, 101)

printf '.venv/
__pycache__/
.pytest_cache/
' > .gitignore && git add -A && git commit -qm start && uv run pytest -q
Plant a bug: sed -i '' 's/(100 - percent)/(100 + percent)/' discount.py (on Linux: sed -i). Then uv run pytest -q test_weak.py
worked.see:
1 passed
(the weak test still passes on broken code)

worked.do: git checkout -q discount.py && git worktree add -q ../lab85-ticket-2 -b ticket-2 && git worktree list

lab.faded: Plant a second bug: change percent > 100 to percent > 101. Predict which test catches it before you run anything. Running the two test files and reading the result is left to you.
lab.alone: Write a 30-minute plan for Training 2 in the shape of the Training 1 plan. Include steps with minutes, one vague and one clear made-up ticket, the pair swap, and where weak plans go.
lab.done: A weak test passed on the planted bug, a strong one failed, two worktrees exist, and your Training 2 plan is written.

quiz.q: A teammate wants 20 agents to implement one feature step by step, each building on the last. What does Training 3 teach?

options.text: Fan out: more agents finish faster.
options.why: Dependent steps do not split; parallel agents would collide or wait.

options.text: Stay with one agent for a chain of dependent steps; fan out for research, review and tests.
options.why: One writer per change, and fan out only where the pieces are independent.

options.text: Set a hard token limit so the run stops at 300k.
options.why: The size in the prompt guides; nothing cuts a run.

quiz.q: Sean assigned a ticket to Nova and reviewed its PR. May he approve it?

options.why: The requester never approves their own agent's PR.
Byte's review is not the human approval; someone other than the requester approves.

options.text: No, someone other than the requester gives the one approval.
options.why: Training 4 makes sure every reviewer knows this.

quiz.q: At office hours, someone says the verify skill did not load after an edit. What should the log say it becomes?

options.text: Nothing; answer the question and move on.
options.why: Most questions should feed the tools.

options.text: A skill line (fix the description) and an eval case that checks it fires.
options.why: The log's last column turns questions into fixes.
A small fix in the skill and a case is cheaper and lasts.

recall: From g8-2: how does verify say you prove a check can fail?
From p8-7: when does running many agents at once help, and when does it hurt?

words.plain: A Claude Code mode where the agent reads and plans but does not edit until you approve.
A second checkout of the same repo in another folder, so two tasks do not collide.
Splitting work across several agents at once; good for independent pieces, bad for dependent steps.
A prompt that says how many agents and roughly how many tokens to use, as guidance, not a limit.
A fixed weekly drop-in slot for questions about skills, plugins and agents.
The person who handed the ticket to Nova; they never approve that PR.
